target:
def Target : Prop :=
  ∀ (Fm S : Type) [LogicalConnective Fm] [LogicalNeutral Fm] [Entailment S Fm] (𝓢 : S) [Entailment.Cl 𝓢]
    (K F : Fm → Fm) (conF : Fm),
    𝓢 ⊢ K conF 🡒 conF →
    𝓢 ⊢ K (∼conF) 🡒 ∼conF →
    𝓢 ⊢ K conF 🡒 F conF →
    𝓢 ⊢ conF 🡒 ∼F conF →
    𝓢 ⊢ ∼K conF ⋏ (conF 🡒 ∼K (∼conF))
a_raw: {"translation": "`Target` is the proposition asserting that for all types `Fm` (of sentences) and `S` (of proof systems), equipped with the formal logical connectives (implication `🡒`, conjunction `⋏`, disjunction `⋎`, negation `∼`) and constants (`⊤`, `⊥`) on `Fm` and a provability relation `⊢` between `S` and `Fm`; for every proof system `𝓢 : S` that proves all classical propositional tautologies in these connectives and is closed under modus ponens; for all arbitrary functions `K, F : Fm → Fm`; and for every sentence `conF : Fm`: if `𝓢` proves all four sentences (1) `(K conF) 🡒 conF`, (2) `(K (∼conF)) 🡒 (∼conF)`, (3) `(K conF) 🡒 (F conF)`, and (4) `conF 🡒 (∼(F conF))`, then `𝓢` proves the sentence `(∼(K conF)) ⋏ (conF 🡒 (∼(K (∼conF))))`. Nothing else is required: `𝓢` is not assumed to be consistent or closed under any rule beyond modus ponens, `K` and `F` are completely arbitrary functions with no axioms assumed about them (such as necessitation or distribution) and are only ever applied to `conF` and `∼conF`, and `conF` is simply an arbitrary sentence in `Fm` rather than a formal consistency statement."}
translation: `Target` is the proposition asserting that for all types `Fm` (of sentences) and `S` (of proof systems), equipped with the formal logical connectives (implication `🡒`, conjunction `⋏`, disjunction `⋎`, negation `∼`) and constants (`⊤`, `⊥`) on `Fm` and a provability relation `⊢` between `S` and `Fm`; for every proof system `𝓢 : S` that proves all classical propositional tautologies in these connectives and is closed under modus ponens; for all arbitrary functions `K, F : Fm → Fm`; and for every sentence `conF : Fm`: if `𝓢` proves all four sentences (1) `(K conF) 🡒 conF`, (2) `(K (∼conF)) 🡒 (∼conF)`, (3) `(K conF) 🡒 (F conF)`, and (4) `conF 🡒 (∼(F conF))`, then `𝓢` proves the sentence `(∼(K conF)) ⋏ (conF 🡒 (∼(K (∼conF))))`. Nothing else is required: `𝓢` is not assumed to be consistent or closed under any rule beyond modus ponens, `K` and `F` are completely arbitrary functions with no axioms assumed about them (such as necessitation or distribution) and are only ever applied to `conF` and `∼conF`, and `conF` is simply an arbitrary sentence in `Fm` rather than a formal consistency statement.

divergences.description: The contingent surpassing hypothesis `K conF 🡒 F conF` is formalized as a meta-level provability premise (`𝓢 ⊢ K conF 🡒 F conF → ...`) uniformly with the DTK principles, rather than as an object-level antecedent (`𝓢 ⊢ (K conF 🡒 F conF) 🡒 ...`) or a side assumption (`K conF 🡒 F conF ⊢_DTK ...`), whereas `conF` in the second conjunct is placed at the object level (`conF 🡒 ∼K (∼conF)`). Because `Target` quantifies over all classical systems `𝓢`, instantiating `𝓢` to `DTK` extended with `K conF 🡒 F conF` makes this logically equivalent, so it is a harmless presentational choice.

judgement.summary: The Lean formalization faithfully captures the author's stated repair of the corollary in the declared abstract setting, matching all four hypotheses and both parts of the two-sided undecidability conclusion exactly. The only minor caveat is the harmless presentational choice of placing the surpassing premise `K conF 🡒 F conF` as a provability hypothesis of `𝓢` rather than an object-level conditional, which is equivalent given universal quantification over classical systems `𝓢`.
